title: Secrets And Lies

jokes.text: Jack sends his assistant to a nonexistent Italian bakery in Queens to get him out of the way
jokes.setup: Jack explains he needed to get his assistant out of the office so he and C.C. could meet secretly
jokes.punchline: He sent him to a nonexistent bakery — an absurdly elaborate lie that highlights Jack's manipulative precision
jokes.explanation: Works because it's perfectly character-specific — Jack would absolutely construct an elaborate fake errand. The specificity of 'nonexistent Italian bakery in Queens' sells it.

jokes.text: Kenneth's assistant arrives panicked: 'This is the address he gave me. He never makes mistakes. I can't go back there without sfogliatelle!'
jokes.setup: Jack mentions he sent his assistant to a nonexistent bakery
jokes.punchline: Kenneth bursts in holding the address, completely panicked about not finding the bakery, playing the gag straight with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure: the setup established the nonexistent bakery, then immediately pays it off with Kenneth's frantic sincerity. 'Sfogliatelle' is a perfectly obscure, specific word for maximum comedy. Kenneth's earnestness ('He never makes mistakes') elevates it. Near-8 territory because of economy, specificity, and character integration.

jokes.text: C.C.'s name tag: 'Lakeesha Gutierrez-Arafat'
jokes.setup: Jack is introducing C.C. under a fake name for discretion
jokes.punchline: The name he chose — Lakeesha Gutierrez-Arafat — is a maximally multicultural, politically provocative fake identity, the opposite of a subtle cover
jokes.explanation: The comedy comes from the irony of Jack — a conservative patrician — choosing this aggressively diverse fake name. It's a compact joke that also satirizes Jack's class and political identity. Maximum economy: three words do everything.

jokes.text: Take off your pants suit. / Right back at you. / Oh! Workplace!
jokes.setup: Jack and C.C. are in a compromising situation; Jack says 'Take off your pants suit'
jokes.punchline: C.C. retorts 'Right back at you' (implying Jack is also wearing something similarly unsexy), then Liz walks in and blurts 'Oh! Workplace!' — a perfectly absurd single-word encapsulation of awkward office intrusion
jokes.explanation: 'Oh! Workplace!' is a genuinely brilliant compression — instead of a full sentence of embarrassed reaction, Liz reduces it to a single noun-as-exclamation. It's perfectly Liz: awkward, over-clinical, and funny precisely because of its economy. The 'Right back at you' also lands as a quick wit beat from C.C.

jokes.text: Liz: 'I like your necklace.' C.C.: 'It's actually a rape whistle but the whistle part fell off, and I just liked how it looked so I kept it.'
jokes.setup: Liz makes polite small talk complimenting C.C.'s necklace
jokes.punchline: C.C. nonchalantly explains it's a broken rape whistle she's repurposed as jewelry — an absurdly casual overshare
jokes.explanation: A perfect subversion of small talk. The deadpan delivery of a dark non sequitur — the whistle part falling off but keeping it as a fashion choice — is both absurdist and character-revealing. Highly quotable and genuinely surprising.

jokes.text: Liz says 'It' meaning business: 'I call the movie Risky Business, Risky It, because 'it' means business.'
jokes.setup: Liz awkwardly says 'I'll leave you to it' and immediately clarifies 'it being business'
jokes.punchline: She then over-explains with her Risky Business/Risky It theory — a bizarre non sequitur that reveals Liz's awkward social spiraling
jokes.explanation: Classic Liz Lemon — socially spiraling into unnecessary explanation. The movie-title wordplay is odd enough to be funny and perfectly captures her awkward oversharing personality.

jokes.text: Liz says 'Lemon out' as she exits — as if signing off from a radio broadcast
jokes.setup: Liz has just made a fool of herself and is leaving the room
jokes.punchline: 'Lemon out' — a self-important sign-off that underscores her obliviousness
jokes.explanation: Two words, maximum character. Perfectly encapsulates Liz's self-serious obliviousness. Very quotable and economical.

jokes.text: Pete to Toofer: 'Hey, take that off. You didn't go to Harvard.' Toofer: 'I went to Harvard.'
jokes.setup: Pete assumes Toofer is wearing a Harvard sweatshirt pretentiously
jokes.punchline: Toofer actually went to Harvard — Pete's presumption backfires
jokes.explanation: A clean reversal that sets up the Harvard running gag. Functional misdirection — we expect Toofer to be a fraud, he isn't.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Well, I got a squeezer from an Indian girl on a bunk bed, so I think I got the full Harvard experience.' Pete: 'That does sound pretty accurate.'
jokes.setup: Pete insists Frank didn't attend Harvard
jokes.punchline: Frank's crude description of his 'Harvard experience' is topped by Pete's deadpan validation of it
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke: Frank's crude punchline is good, but Pete's straight-faced 'That does sound pretty accurate' is the real gem — it validates the joke while subverting Pete's own elitism.

jokes.text: Jack: 'That woman you met this morning in my office is not a colleague of mine. We are lovers.' Liz: 'Oh, that word bums me out unless it's between the words meat and pizza.'
jokes.setup: Jack uses the word 'lovers' to describe his relationship with C.C.
jokes.punchline: Liz's specific objection — the only acceptable usage is 'meat lovers pizza' — is perfectly Liz: food-obsessed, prudish about intimacy
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best. The 'meat lovers pizza' specification is both an instant Liz character summary and a genuinely original construction. The specific placement ('between the words') shows real craft. Could only be Liz Lemon. Highly quotable and a callback target later in the episode.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Okay, if I can't say lovers, you can't say feelings.'
jokes.setup: Liz asks if Jack has 'serious feelings' for C.C. after he revealed she bums him out with 'lovers'
jokes.punchline: Jack applies Liz's same word-objection logic symmetrically — 'feelings' is his equivalent forbidden word
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback that immediately tops the previous joke. Jack turning Liz's complaint back on her with symmetrical logic is character-perfect — he's emotionally unavailable but intellectually sharp. Very quotable. Strong structure.

jokes.text: This corporation has a very strict 'bros before hos' policy.
jokes.setup: Jack is explaining why his relationship with C.C. is complicated — she's trying to destroy his company
jokes.punchline: He describes the conflict in corporate-memo language: a formal 'bros before hos' policy
jokes.explanation: The comedy comes entirely from register collision: Jack's formal, patrician corporate-speak applied to street slang. Only Jack Donaghy would describe loyalty to his male executive peers as a formal policy with the phrase 'bros before hos.' The joke is specific to his character and couldn't land in the mouth of anyone else.

jokes.text: Liz: 'Oh, come on! I don't have that. Very hairy.'
jokes.setup: Jack has just accused Liz of having alopecia
jokes.punchline: Liz's protest — 'Very hairy' — is both defensive and bizarrely specific, implying she's hairy in ways that make the denial worse
jokes.explanation: The callback reaction is the real punchline. 'Very hairy' as a defense is both self-undermining and perfectly Liz — she can't stop herself from oversharing even when the overshare makes things worse.

jokes.text: Jenna wins 'Best Actress in a Movie Based on a Musical Based on a Movie'
jokes.setup: Jenna announces she won an award for a film adaptation
jokes.punchline: The award category is 'Best Actress in a Movie Based on a Musical Based on a Movie' — a maximally recursive, meaningless distinction
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed absurdist joke about Hollywood derivative culture. The three-layer recursion (movie → musical → movie) is both a skewering of award-show inflation and a perfect Jenna beat — she would be proud of this meaningless honor. Economy is excellent; the whole joke is the title.

jokes.text: Tracy storms in: 'Okay, enough! How long are we going to talk about this stupid award? We have more important things to worry about. Like where are the french fries I did not ask for? You guys need to anticipate me.'
jokes.setup: The writers are discussing Jenna's award
jokes.punchline: Tracy erupts about something 'more important' — which turns out to be french fries he didn't ask for but expects to have been anticipated
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly Tracy: the righteous indignation about something trivially self-centered, the absurd 'you guys need to anticipate me' logic. The joke requires no setup beyond knowing Tracy Jordan exists. The specificity of 'french fries I did not ask for' is pure Tracy id.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'It's not fair, Liz Lemon. Everybody wins awards but me. Even Shaquille O'Neal got a Kids' Choice Award for that animated movie we did.'
jokes.setup: Tracy is jealous of Jenna's award
jokes.punchline: He cites Shaquille O'Neal's Kids' Choice Award as evidence of cosmic injustice — making Shaq his peer in the grievance
jokes.explanation: The joke works on Tracy's oblivious logic — he's more upset about Shaq than Jenna, and citing a Kids' Choice Award as high artistic achievement is perfect character work.

jokes.text: Cutaway to animated Shaq movie clip: 'Boy, I hope we rescue the Starfish King on this adventure.' 'It'll be a slam dunk!'
jokes.setup: Tracy mentions an animated movie he did with Shaquille O'Neal
jokes.punchline: The clip shows Shaq's character saying 'It'll be a slam dunk!' — a groan-worthy basketball pun in a children's movie, exactly as bad as you'd expect
jokes.explanation: The joke-within-a-joke: the animated clip is intentionally terrible, and the basketball pun is deliberately groan-worthy. The meta-layer of it being shown as a legitimately bad movie is the real joke.

jokes.text: Non-sequitur line from animated movie: 'Would you call what we did last night sex?'
jokes.setup: We're watching a clip from an apparently innocent animated children's movie
jokes.punchline: A completely inappropriate line appears in what should be a kids' film — a jarring non sequitur that implies wildly adult content
jokes.explanation: Perfectly timed absurdist bomb dropped into an apparently innocent animated clip. The economy is extraordinary — one line of dialogue does all the work. The contrast between children's movie context and adult content is maximally jarring.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'A million dollars, a yellow Bentley, and nothing. I never win anything!'
jokes.setup: Tracy complains he got nothing from the animated movie
jokes.punchline: He lists 'a million dollars and a yellow Bentley' as 'nothing' — complete obliviousness to what counts as compensation
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character economy: 'A million dollars, a yellow Bentley, and nothing' — the 'and nothing' completing the list as if those prior things don't count. This is pure Tracy logic at its finest and reveals his child-mind relationship to money vs. validation.

jokes.text: Tracy holds up a coffee mug his kids got him for Father's Day that says 'I'm a failure'
jokes.setup: Tracy is trying to prove he's underappreciated
jokes.punchline: The mug literally says 'I'm a failure' — his kids gave him an inadvertently devastating Father's Day gift
jokes.explanation: Visual gag that requires no explanation — the mug is the whole joke. Dark and absurd: his children either know him well or accidentally destroyed him. The ambiguity makes it richer.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'Maybe I should just give up and try this crystal meth I've been hearing so much about.'
jokes.setup: Tracy is spiraling into self-pity about never winning awards
jokes.punchline: His solution to professional disappointment is to 'try crystal meth' — framed as a reasonable next step, like trying a new restaurant
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'I've been hearing so much about' is perfect — it positions crystal meth as a hot new lifestyle trend Tracy is curious to explore, like a spa treatment. The casual framing is the joke. Strong character integration (only Tracy) and highly quotable.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'Pacific Rim? I love the Pacific Rim. I spent nine months in Japan shooting Samurai, I-Am-Urai.'
jokes.setup: Liz tells Tracy he's getting a lifetime achievement award from the Pacific Rim Emmys
jokes.punchline: Tracy's film title 'Samurai, I-Am-Urai' — a phonetic pun that also implies a deeply silly movie
jokes.explanation: The movie title is an obvious pun ('Samurai / I Am Urai') but it works because the phonetic construction is earnest. Tracy would make this film and be proud of this title.

jokes.text: Tracy explains 'sharking' — running up on a lady and pulling her tube top down while a friend videotapes. 'It's considered a crime here. Thanks a lot, Puritans.'
jokes.setup: Tracy says he fell in love with Japanese culture, especially 'sharking'
jokes.punchline: Sharking is a real/absurd Japanese prank — and Tracy blames the Puritans for its illegality in America, a wildly misplaced historical complaint
jokes.explanation: Two-beat joke: the explanation of sharking is shocking-funny, and 'Thanks a lot, Puritans' is a perfect capper. Tracy's historical grievance is absurd misdirection. The Puritans-as-culprit framing is inventive.

jokes.text: Liz to Pete: 'He's fine. I just need you to make him a Pacific Rim Emmy.' Pete: 'Props has an old basketball trophy we could solder some wings onto.'
jokes.setup: Liz explains Tracy's award isn't real and she needs a fake trophy made
jokes.punchline: Pete's immediate, practical solution — a basketball trophy with wings soldered on — suggests this kind of improvisation is completely routine
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Pete's blasé readiness — 'Props has an old basketball trophy we could solder some wings onto' implies they've done this or similar before. The specificity of 'wings' (as in Emmy wings) is nice craft.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'I don't get that kind of treatment.' Liz: 'I don't have to treat you that way because you're the sane one. You're my rock.' Jenna: 'It is amazing how grounded I've been able to stay despite my célébrité.'
jokes.setup: Liz tells Jenna she doesn't coddle her because Jenna is the sane, grounded one
jokes.punchline: Jenna accepts this completely unironically while using 'célébrité' (the French/pretentious version of 'celebrity'), undermining the claim immediately
jokes.explanation: The joke has a beautiful three-part structure: Liz's lie, Jenna's credulous acceptance, and then her self-sabotage with 'célébrité.' The French word does everything — it confirms Jenna is exactly as ungrounded as Tracy, just differently delusional. Very Jenna-specific.

jokes.text: Frank walks up to Toofer with a Harvard sweatshirt on: 'What's up, dude? I went to Harvard.'
jokes.setup: Earlier Pete established only Toofer went to Harvard; Frank tried to claim it
jokes.punchline: Frank has now acquired a Harvard sweatshirt and is using it to claim membership — escalating his Harvard fraud
jokes.explanation: Running gag escalation: Frank is now fully committed to the Harvard bit. Straightforward but funny because of Frank's total commitment.

jokes.text: It is amazing how grounded I've been able to stay despite my célébrité.
jokes.setup: Liz calls Jenna 'grounded'
jokes.punchline: Jenna immediately claims credit for being grounded, using the pretentious Frenchified 'célébrité' — a word that reveals she is exactly as ungrounded as expected
jokes.explanation: The use of the French 'célébrité' instead of 'celebrity' is the joke — it's simultaneously pretentious and the most obvious possible tell that Jenna is not actually grounded. The self-congratulation about grounded-ness while using a self-aggrandizing French term is perfectly self-defeating. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Toofer produces the Signet Society pin, Pete produces the same pin from his pocket, Toofer says 'Oh, you mean this pin?' — and Pete points out 'Your lame thing is on his pants.'
jokes.setup: Toofer tries to expose Frank's Harvard fraud by producing an exclusive Harvard society pin
jokes.punchline: Frank already has the Signet Society pin on his pants — the ultimate one-upping that makes no logical sense and is funnier for it
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation of the Harvard gag. The pin on his PANTS — not lapel, not hat — is an absurd visual detail. Pete's 'your lame thing is on his pants' line is the capper. The absurdity of Frank somehow having the exclusive Signet pin is funnier than any logical explanation.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'Perfect. Just when I get back from Maiden Voyage, Newark's first offshore gentlemen's barge.'
jokes.setup: Liz says the ceremony will be at 4:00 in the morning due to time zone difference
jokes.punchline: Tracy is already planning to be at 'Maiden Voyage, Newark's first offshore gentlemen's barge' — an absurdly specific strip club concept
jokes.explanation: The specificity is extraordinary: 'Maiden Voyage' (perfect name), 'Newark's first' (implies a demand for more), 'offshore gentlemen's barge' (a floating strip club that navigates around New Jersey jurisdiction). This is 30 Rock at its finest — a throwaway line packed with institutional comedy.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'Liz Lemon know who keeps the lights on around here. But I couldn't do it without my background players.'
jokes.setup: Tracy magnanimously thanks Liz and Josh for supporting him
jokes.punchline: He calls them 'background players' — a term from film/TV that reduces them to extras in his life story
jokes.explanation: The 'background players' characterization is a nice Tracy-ism — he's being magnanimous while still dehumanizing the people he's thanking.

jokes.text: Tracy offers to let Liz and Josh 'hold' his award, then says 'Then you can check out my award. Ha ha ha! Banter!'
jokes.setup: Tracy magnanimously promises to let Liz hold his award
jokes.punchline: He announces his own joke as 'Banter!' — labeling his attempted wit like a social media hashtag, completely unaware of what banter actually is
jokes.explanation: Tracy narrating his own social performance is perfect character comedy. Announcing 'Banter!' after a weak innuendo is Tracy at his most self-deluded and endearing. The meta-label is a uniquely Tracy way to interact with humor. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Jenna says 'I can't even get a real exterminator to get that squirrel out of my dressing room.' — followed immediately by the sound of squirrel chaos
jokes.setup: Jenna complains about not getting the same treatment as Tracy
jokes.punchline: She mentions the squirrel problem right before it apparently attacks her — 'No! No, don't move like that! No, no! Ow!'
jokes.explanation: The immediate callback (mentioning the squirrel, then getting immediately attacked) is a tight structural joke. 'Don't move like that!' is great because it implies the squirrel is making deliberate, threatening choices.

jokes.text: Jack to C.C. about the dinner guest list: 'We had to eliminate anybody with any influence or connections or stature, so that pretty much left you. Then we added Kenneth so you would have somebody to talk to.'
jokes.setup: Liz asks if this is everyone at the dinner party
jokes.punchline: Jack explains the process of elimination that ended with only Liz — and adds Kenneth as Liz's conversation companion, implying they're both at the bottom of his social hierarchy
jokes.explanation: Classic Jack — the insult is wrapped in politeness, but the logic is devastating. The 'then we added Kenneth' capper is perfect: Liz and Kenneth being social equals in Jack's world is both funny and subtly dark.

jokes.text: Kenneth awkwardly tries to make conversation with Liz: 'What's your favorite pizza topping? Mine's plain, but I like others.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth has been added to the dinner so Liz has someone to talk to
jokes.punchline: His icebreaker is 'What's your favorite pizza topping?' — with his answer being 'plain,' an impossibly earnest and social-skill-free conversation starter
jokes.explanation: 'Mine's plain, but I like others' is a perfect Kenneth line — it has the warmth, the earnestness, and the complete social obliviousness that defines him. He's trying to do diplomacy with pizza topping diplomacy.

jokes.text: Jack to Liz, completely sincerely: 'I have to say, you are the most beautiful woman in this room right now.'
jokes.setup: Jack makes what sounds like a compliment to Liz at the dinner party
jokes.punchline: The phrase 'in this room right now' is doing enormous work — C.C. is clearly present, meaning this is a precisely qualified non-compliment
jokes.explanation: A subtly constructed insult-compliment. The qualifier 'in this room right now' means Jack is complimenting Liz only relative to C.C., implying Liz is less beautiful in all other contexts. Classic Jack precision.

jokes.text: Kenneth asks Liz: 'Tell me a painful story about your teenage years.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth is trying to make conversation with Liz at the dinner party
jokes.punchline: His conversation gambit shifts from pizza toppings to demanding painful teenage confessions — an extreme tonal leap that reveals his total social naivety
jokes.explanation: The contrast between the sweet pizza question and this emotionally invasive follow-up is perfect Kenneth escalation. He's not malicious — he genuinely thinks this is good conversation. Also funny because Liz clearly has many such stories.

jokes.text: Tracy opens his acceptance speech: 'People of the Pacific Rim, how you feel?'
jokes.setup: Tracy is delivering a fake acceptance speech via satellite to a fake awards show
jokes.punchline: He opens with a concert-style crowd call — inappropriate register for an awards acceptance speech, especially one to a Japanese audience via satellite
jokes.explanation: Tracy treating an awards ceremony like a hip-hop concert is pure character. The 'how you feel?' to a Japanese satellite audience is especially absurd.

jokes.text: Tracy thanks 'a very special blond lady — Shelley Long, you're truly an inspiration to me!'
jokes.setup: Tracy says he wants to thank 'a very special blond lady' — everyone expects Jenna
jokes.punchline: He thanks Shelley Long from Cheers — completely blindsiding Jenna who is standing right there
jokes.explanation: Exceptional misdirection. The 'very special blond lady' setup builds genuine anticipation for Jenna's moment, then annihilates it with Shelley Long — a specific, random, perfectly Tracy choice. The brutality of the snub is the joke. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: Karaoke, karate, and most of all... wanizame atakku! / Shark attack!
jokes.setup: Tracy is thanking the Pacific Rim for its cultural contributions
jokes.punchline: After listing karaoke and karate (real cultural exports), he says the greatest gift was 'shark attack' — a callback to sharking, delivered in Japanese with a subtitle
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback structure. The list of Japanese cultural contributions sets up a formal gratitude convention, then 'shark attack' (i.e., the sexual harassment practice) as the 'most of all' gift is a great subversion. Delivering it in Japanese with a subtitle adds the perfect absurdist layer. The callback rewards attentive viewers.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'How could Tracy not thank me? I drag myself out of bed at 4:00 in the morning, go home, get dressed, come in here, and he doesn't even mention my name?' Liz: 'Jenna, the whole thing is fake.' Jenna: 'Yeah, but he thought it was real.'
jokes.setup: Jenna is furious Tracy didn't thank her in his acceptance speech
jokes.punchline: Liz points out the ceremony is fake; Jenna's comeback — 'yeah, but he thought it was real' — is both logically correct and reveals her bottomless narcissistic wound
jokes.explanation: Jenna's 'yeah, but he thought it was real' is a perfect Jenna line — she's technically correct, which makes it both funny and a character revelation. She needs the validation even when the ceremony is fake. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Liz: 'I did hear the janitor saying your boobs looked good.'
jokes.setup: Jenna is devastated by Tracy's snub
jokes.punchline: Liz offers this as consolation — a completely inappropriate, off-brand compliment relayed from the janitor, delivered as if it helps
jokes.explanation: The specificity of the janitor as source makes it funnier — Liz is genuinely trying and this is the best she's got. The deadpan delivery of it as comfort is perfect Liz.

jokes.text: The squirrel reappears in Jenna's dressing room: 'Aah! The squirrel! It's not afraid of people!'
jokes.setup: Earlier Jenna mentioned the squirrel in her dressing room; now she's being attacked again
jokes.punchline: 'It's not afraid of people!' — the squirrel has agency and menace
jokes.explanation: Running gag payoff. The line 'It's not afraid of people' anthropomorphizes the squirrel in a way that's funnier than a simple attack. A serviceable callback but not elevated beyond the original.

jokes.text: C.C. and Liz play a game where they apparently finish each other's celebrity references without speaking. 'Venus Williams.' 'Remember that time you fell asleep?' 'Captain Beefheart.'
jokes.setup: C.C. approaches Liz to talk about Jack and they discover they get along suspiciously well
jokes.punchline: Their conversation is completely non sequitur — they're apparently playing a game or sharing references that make sense only to them, with 'Captain Beefheart' as the capper
jokes.explanation: The absurdist non sequitur game between C.C. and Liz suggests instant rapport through shared chaotic reference points. 'Captain Beefheart' as the third beat is a perfect escalation — obscure enough to be funny, specific enough to feel real.

jokes.text: The Charades game at the dinner party: 'This is not a character from a television program.' 'Okay. This is not a character from the Bible.' 'Uh, pass.' 'You can't pass, you hillbilly!'
jokes.setup: C.C. and Liz are playing what appears to be a reference game at the dinner party
jokes.punchline: 'You can't pass, you hillbilly!' — C.C.'s sudden aggression when Liz passes, revealing C.C.'s competitive edge
jokes.explanation: The escalation from calm game-playing to 'you hillbilly!' is a fun character reveal for C.C. — her liberal veneer cracks into something authentically human when her charades integrity is threatened.

jokes.text: C.C. slaps Liz: 'No. I'm sorry. I don't normally slap people.'
jokes.setup: C.C. has been playing a heated charades-style game with Liz
jokes.punchline: C.C. slaps Liz and then immediately disclaims it as out of character — the apology is funnier than the slap
jokes.explanation: 'I don't normally slap people' is funnier than the slap itself — it's such a specific, unusual disclaimer that it raises more questions about C.C.'s history than it answers.

jokes.text: In C.C. and Liz's conversation, out of nowhere: 'I'm-a the plumber. I'm here-a to fix the washing machine.' 'Come right in, Mr. Spunatelli.'
jokes.setup: C.C. and Liz are having a serious conversation about Jack
jokes.punchline: They slip into what is apparently the beginning of a porno scenario ('plumber comes to fix washing machine') delivered completely straight
jokes.explanation: This is brilliantly weird — the two women apparently have a spontaneous bit they do together mid-serious-conversation. 'Mr. Spunatelli' is a perfect pornographic Italian name. The non sequitur delivery in a serious emotional scene is the whole joke.

jokes.text: Liz: 'I don't think you want to take advice from me. I ate a 3 Musketeers bar for breakfast this morning, and this bra is held together with tape.'
jokes.setup: C.C. asks Liz for relationship advice about Jack
jokes.punchline: Liz's self-disqualification via 3 Musketeers breakfast and tape-reinforced bra — two specific, escalating details of personal chaos
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Liz Lemon jokes. The pairing of 3 Musketeers breakfast (food slovenliness) with tape-bra (physical disorganization) is a perfect two-beat portrait of Liz. The tape bra is a callback later when C.C. mentions it to Jack. Extremely quotable and character-defining.

jokes.text: C.C. and Liz simultaneously: 'Me either.' Then Liz: 'Oh God, it was my birthday yesterday.'
jokes.setup: C.C. says she's never compromised for a man; Liz agrees she hasn't either
jokes.punchline: Liz's immediate follow-up — 'Oh God, it was my birthday yesterday' — is delivered as a gut-punch of self-awareness about her lonely life
jokes.explanation: The 'Oh God, it was my birthday yesterday' is delivered as a non sequitur but lands as a perfect dark punchline: she admitted she's never compromised for a man, then immediately realized she spent her birthday alone. Six words, maximum existential weight. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Hey, guys, it's me... Frank. / Oh, no. Escalation!
jokes.setup: Frank enters wearing a hat like Toofer's, escalating their hat/dress rivalry
jokes.punchline: Someone immediately names the narrative beat: 'Escalation!' — meta-awareness of their own conflict's structure
jokes.explanation: The meta-commentary on their own feud's escalation structure is a quick, sharp meta joke. 'Escalation!' as a one-word reaction beat is good economy. The feud subplot is the episode's weakest, but this beat works.

jokes.text: Frank's mom is invoked in the hat insult; Frank defends her: 'My mom's a great lady.' Toofer: 'Was it her greatness that made your dad leave?'
jokes.setup: Frank defends his mom from an insult about his hat
jokes.punchline: Toofer escalates with the nuclear option: suggesting Frank's mom's greatness drove his dad away
jokes.explanation: A sharp insult with good structure, but fairly conventional in its approach. The construction 'Was it her greatness that made your dad leave?' is well-turned but doesn't rise above a standard TV comeback.

jokes.text: Frank: 'He didn't leave. He's a submarine commander running silent.'
jokes.setup: Toofer implies Frank's dad abandoned the family
jokes.punchline: Frank's defensive comeback — his dad is a 'submarine commander running silent' — is a child's magical thinking dressed up in naval terminology
jokes.explanation: Exceptional. 'Running silent' is real submarine terminology, which makes Frank's desperate lie more specific and therefore more heartbreaking and funny. It's absurdist childhood rationalization delivered with adult conviction. Very quotable. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: Jack: '$5 million each? That's NBA sexual-assault money.'
jokes.setup: C.C. tells Jack the Sheinhardt Wig plaintiffs settled for $5 million each
jokes.punchline: Jack's immediate reference frame for '$5 million each' is NBA sexual-assault settlements — a dark, specific, perfectly Jack characterization
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. The specificity of 'NBA sexual-assault money' as a unit of currency is shocking, dark, and perfectly Jack Donaghy — he has an institutional understanding of how scandal settlements work, and $5 million calibrates to this exact bucket for him. Economic, quotable, character-defining.

jokes.text: Jack: 'I like when a woman has ambition. It's like seeing a dog wearing clothes.'
jokes.setup: C.C. says she won't apologize for being ambitious
jokes.punchline: Jack says he likes female ambition — but the compliment is that it's like 'a dog wearing clothes': amusing, somewhat impressive, fundamentally ridiculous
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke. It's a perfectly constructed Jack Donaghy line: starts as what sounds like a progressive statement, reveals itself as deeply condescending, and uses an original, specific image ('dog wearing clothes') that's both funny and devastating. The simile is uniquely Jack — it acknowledges the achievement while denying the legitimacy. It's quotable, it's character-perfect, it captures the show's satirical politics in one sentence. Justifies a 9+.

jokes.text: C.C.: 'I should never have listened to a woman who tapes her bra together.' — calling back Liz's earlier confession
jokes.setup: C.C. is angry at Jack for not going public with their relationship
jokes.punchline: She blames Liz — and specifically the tape bra detail — as evidence that Liz was unqualified advice-giver
jokes.explanation: Strong callback. The tape bra was established as a Liz character detail; C.C. weaponizing it now shows both that she listened and that the detail was specific enough to stick. Good structural callback.

jokes.text: Background TV ad: 'Everybody looks good in a Sheinhardt.'
jokes.setup: The Sheinhardt Wig Company (the sinister parent company of the TV network) has just been referenced in the context of a lawsuit about turning children orange
jokes.punchline: A Sheinhardt wig commercial plays in the background — cheerfully ironic given what we just learned about the company
jokes.explanation: A clever background gag that rewards attentive viewers. The Sheinhardt Wig Company is one of the show's recurring satirical institutions, and having their cheerful ad play after a scene about their orange-children lawsuit is pointed irony.

jokes.text: Jenna has acquired an entourage: 'I'm Sacha. This is Patrice and Master Alexei.' ...and then 'And your name is probably something like Melissa.'
jokes.setup: Jenna has decided to act more like Tracy by getting an entourage
jokes.punchline: Her entourage member immediately and confidently insults Liz by guessing her name is 'Melissa' — a generic, deliberately forgettable name — as if it's a perfectly calibrated put-down
jokes.explanation: 'Master Alexei' is inherently funny (the 'Master' title suggesting either a child or a sex pest), and the Melissa insult is a great character move — it's a showbiz dismissal (calling an assistant/nobody by a generic name). The specificity of 'Melissa' over 'Karen' or 'Jennifer' makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Sacha (entourage member): 'Oh, Melissa? Your face is on the phone. Soccer practice is over and you need to pick it up.'
jokes.setup: Sacha has been insulting Liz throughout the scene
jokes.punchline: The final insult levels up: 'your face is on the phone' combines an insult about Liz's face with a mundane soccer-practice parenting detail — implying Liz is an embarrassing suburban mom-type
jokes.explanation: The 'your face is on the phone / soccer practice' insult is genuinely creative — it conflates a phone insult with suburban-mom imagery in a way that's specific and unexpected. Liz's own acknowledgment 'That's a pretty good burn, Patrice' is also funny.

jokes.text: Liz, grudgingly: 'All right, that's a pretty good burn, Patrice.'
jokes.setup: Sacha/Patrice has just delivered a surprisingly good insult at Liz
jokes.punchline: Liz, who has been the target of the insult, begrudgingly compliments its quality — she can't help but be a fair critic even when being roasted
jokes.explanation: Five words that are pure Liz Lemon. Her inability to not give fair professional feedback even to someone insulting her is character-perfect. Very economical and quotable.

jokes.text: Jack and C.C. spot James Carville in the elevator. Jack asks: 'How do you and Mary Matalin make it work? She's a brilliant, patriotic Republican strategist, and you, let's face it, are a pinko nutjob.'
jokes.setup: Jack needs advice on his cross-partisan relationship
jokes.punchline: He frames the question as 'she's brilliant' vs. 'you are a pinko nutjob' — the asymmetric description is both honest Jack Donaghy and funny in its face
jokes.explanation: Works on the Carville-as-himself level (the joke requires recognition) and on the Jack level — he describes Matalin with admiration and Carville with cheerful contempt while asking him for help. Classic Jack.

jokes.text: James Carville: 'Mary and I have proved that true love can weather any storm. Even Desert Storm.' — 'Cajun style.'
jokes.setup: Carville is giving sincere advice about cross-partisan relationships
jokes.punchline: 'Even Desert Storm' — a Gulf War pun/reference delivered deadpan, followed by Carville's repeated 'Cajun style' catchphrase
jokes.explanation: The Desert Storm pun is nicely deployed — it sounds like an ordinary idiom until the specific war reference lands. 'Cajun style' as Carville's recurring tag is a running gag that escalates through the scene.

jokes.text: 'Cajun style' repeated three times as Carville's punctuation throughout the advice scene
jokes.setup: Carville keeps appending 'Cajun style' to his advice, treating it as universal wisdom seasoning
jokes.punchline: By the third 'Cajun style,' it has become an absurd verbal tic that undercuts everything he says
jokes.explanation: The running-gag structure of 'Cajun style' gets funnier each time it's deployed. By the third use — right after deep psychological insight — it undercuts the profundity perfectly.

jokes.text: Carville: 'Jack, is it really the opinion of others you're worried about, or are you learning something new about yourself and you find that a little scary?' — beat — 'Cajun style.'
jokes.setup: Carville delivers what sounds like a genuinely perceptive psychological observation
jokes.punchline: 'Cajun style' immediately after a heartfelt insight — the tonal whiplash deflates the sincerity into comedy
jokes.explanation: The best use of the 'Cajun style' running gag: Carville says something genuinely insightful, pauses for weight, then 'Cajun style' collapses the emotional reality. The pause before it is the key structural element.

jokes.text: Frank/Toofer feud: 'If we give up our feud now, we'll be ridiculed. Remember when Lutz cried during that diamond commercial? It'd be worse than that.'
jokes.setup: Frank and Toofer are trapped in their feud and trying to figure out how to end it
jokes.punchline: The reference point for maximum humiliation is 'when Lutz cried during that diamond commercial' — Lutz's defining moment of vulnerability becomes the episode's background mythology
jokes.explanation: The Lutz-crying-at-a-diamond-commercial detail is an excellent throwaway world-building joke — it implies this is a well-known office event with specific social consequences. The choice of 'diamond commercial' is perfect (it's the sappiest, most emotionally manipulative ad genre).

jokes.text: Carville advises Frank/Toofer: 'You need to change the story, like Karl Rove did in the last election when he made it about gay folks and swift boats. What's your swift boat?' — then: 'You didn't hear this from me, but Josh is starting to do something new with his hair.'
jokes.setup: Carville is advising Frank and Toofer on political strategy to escape their feud
jokes.punchline: He applies Karl Rove's distracting-the-media tactics to a petty writers' room feud, then delivers actionable intelligence about Josh's haircut
jokes.explanation: The joke has perfect structural levels: applying high-stakes political strategy to a trivial writers' room beef, then the operationally specific 'you didn't hear this from me, but Josh is starting to do something new with his hair.' Carville is a political spymaster leaking hair intel. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Carville tries to steal candy from a vending machine; Liz watches. Carville: 'Let me show you how it's done. Cajun style.'
jokes.setup: Carville runs into Liz trying to steal from a vending machine
jokes.punchline: He offers to demonstrate the skill — 'Cajun style' — applying his brand of mysterious Southern expertise to a vending machine theft
jokes.explanation: The final 'Cajun style' use is funny because it's applied to the smallest possible context (vending machine theft) after being applied to political strategy and relationship advice. The escalating absurdity of what 'Cajun style' covers is the gag.

jokes.text: Tracy to Liz: 'I'm gonna take a nap. Wake me up if Andy Dick calls.'
jokes.setup: Tracy is still acting difficult in response to Jenna's difficult behavior
jokes.punchline: 'Wake me up if Andy Dick calls' — Andy Dick as the threshold of urgency, implying he's both dangerous enough and interesting enough to interrupt a nap for
jokes.explanation: The Andy Dick reference works on multiple levels — Dick was a well-known Hollywood troublemaker at this time, and Tracy treating his call as a priority is perfectly Tracy. The economy is excellent: eight words, full character.

jokes.text: Liz reveals she secretly runs Jenna's fan club as a punishment for a writer: 'That's me. I made Frank set that up as a punishment after he farted in my chair.'
jokes.setup: Liz is listing all the ways she secretly coddles Jenna
jokes.punchline: Her online fan club is something she had Frank set up as punishment for farting in her chair — two reveals in one sentence (fake fan club + farting as the punishment trigger)
jokes.explanation: This joke works on several levels simultaneously: it reveals the fan club is fake (funny), explains WHY it was created (funnier — Frank farted in her chair), and shows Liz's elaborate, petty justice system. The layered reveal structure is excellent.

jokes.text: Liz describes secretly calling in to Jenna's morning radio show as all the callers: 'every caller was me. I am loving all of your characters. Thanks for calling, Sanjay. I really believe in Karma.'
jokes.setup: Liz continues listing her secret Jenna-coddling activities
jokes.punchline: She performed every caller on a morning radio show — including 'Sanjay' — demonstrating an enormous amount of effort for a completely unnecessary deception
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Sanjay' and 'I really believe in Karma' — a caller Liz invented and then performed with a full character voice on live radio — is excellent. It reveals both the depth of Liz's enabling and the absurdity of her efforts. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Liz: 'And this award you just got? It's a cookie.' Jenna: 'Ooh, crunch!'
jokes.setup: Liz reveals the award Jenna won is also fake/a prop
jokes.punchline: Jenna, instead of feeling insulted, bites the award and comments 'Ooh, crunch!' — she's delighted it's an actual cookie
jokes.explanation: Perfect three-beat: 'It's a cookie' is the reveal, Jenna biting it is the physical action, 'Ooh, crunch!' is the character punchline. Jenna's delight — rather than offense — is the real joke, and it perfectly encapsulates her vanity coexisting with childlike impulsiveness. Extremely economical: two words deliver the entire joke. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: Liz's monologue: 'I don't sleep, I don't eat right, thanks to you and Tracy Jordan. Mostly you.'
jokes.setup: Liz is finally venting her frustrations to Jenna
jokes.punchline: 'Mostly you' — Liz's addendum ranking Jenna worse than Tracy Jordan in terms of her suffering
jokes.explanation: Two words — 'Mostly you' — do enormous work as a capper to a list that already includes Tracy Jordan. The ranking of Jenna as worse than Tracy is a sharp character judgment delivered with maximum economy.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'Oh, Liz. That's all I wanted to hear. I'll be onstage in 10.'
jokes.setup: Liz has just unleashed years of frustration and exhaustion at Jenna
jokes.punchline: Jenna was apparently satisfied by the confession — 'that's all I wanted to hear' — treating Liz's breakdown as the emotional validation she needed
jokes.explanation: Brilliant character reversal: all Jenna wanted was proof that Liz cared enough to suffer for her. The entire breakdown scene was Jenna's real need. 'I'll be onstage in 10' — flipping back to professional normalcy — is perfectly timed. Very Jenna.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'And I'll wait till tomorrow to talk about you firing melon-ball lady.' Liz: 'All right.' Jenna: 'Not in front of the gays.'
jokes.setup: Jenna is wrapping up their conversation with follow-up demands
jokes.punchline: 'Not in front of the gays' — a completely unexplained injunction that implies there are gay people present whose knowledge of melon-ball lady's firing would be a problem
jokes.explanation: 'Not in front of the gays' is an absurd Jenna-ism that needs no explanation to be funny. It implies both a complex social web and Jenna's theatrical performer-identity. Four words, maximum absurdist character comedy.

jokes.text: Frank and Toofer's feud is resolved because Josh got a frohawk: 'Hey, look who bailed on their lame feud.' — beat — 'Dude, you got a frohawk, man. Do you think you're better than us?'
jokes.setup: Frank and Toofer's feud has been a running storyline; Carville advised them to redirect attention to Josh's hair
jokes.punchline: The plan works instantly — they drop their entire feud the moment they see Josh's frohawk and unite in mockery
jokes.explanation: Strong structural payoff to the Carville advice callback. Carville's political strategy works with comic perfection — the absurdity of his advice being correct is the joke. 'Do you think you're better than us?' uniting Frank and Toofer over Josh's haircut is a satisfying resolution.

jokes.text: Josh: 'It's not even my normal barber. My mom did it.' The writers: 'Dr. Haircut!'
jokes.setup: Josh tries to explain the frohawk
jokes.punchline: 'Dr. Haircut' as his new nickname — coined and immediately deployed with commitment — then Josh's 'are you gonna cry?'
jokes.explanation: 'Dr. Haircut' is a great nickname — it's specific enough to be commitment comedy, and the fact that his mom gave it to him makes the 'Dr.' honorific funnier. Josh's sad 'are you gonna cry?' reversal is a good capper.

jokes.text: C.C. uses the John Legend CD as a pretense to see Jack: 'I don't know why it was so urgent you have it before noon.' C.C.: 'It was just an excuse.'
jokes.setup: Jack has C.C.'s assistant deliver a John Legend CD urgently
jokes.punchline: C.C. immediately blows the cover — it was just an excuse — and Jack doesn't try to maintain it
jokes.explanation: A functional comedy beat — Jack uses a John Legend CD as cover (implying he's too dignified for something so romantic) and C.C. cuts through it immediately. Mild chuckle territory.

jokes.text: C.C.: 'I'm 43, and you have great hair. I can let this play out a little longer.'
jokes.setup: Jack asks if C.C. trusts him and proposes a plan
jokes.punchline: C.C.'s decision logic: she's 43 and Jack has great hair — therefore she can tolerate more uncertainty
jokes.explanation: A beautifully honest line: 'I'm 43 and you have great hair' cuts through all the political drama to pure human calculus. The juxtaposition of age-anxiety with such a shallow variable (his hair) is both funny and unexpectedly touching. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Jack: 'C.C., these people are my peers, my heroes, my past and future Secret Santas.'
jokes.setup: Jack brings C.C. to his executive dining room to introduce her publicly
jokes.punchline: 'My past and future Secret Santas' — the list escalates from 'peers' and 'heroes' to this corporate intimacy detail
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy and character specificity. The list builds ('peers, heroes') then collapses into 'past and future Secret Santas' — which reveals more about Jack's inner world than any dramatic monologue could. His deepest relationships are institutionalized gift-exchanges. Very quotable. Near-top tier.

jokes.text: Jack's public announcement: 'She's my liberal, hippy-dippy mama. My groovy chick. My old lady. She wants to tax us all to death and make it legal for a man to marry his own dog.'
jokes.setup: Jack announces C.C. to his conservative colleagues as his partner
jokes.punchline: He characterizes her politics with escalating absurdism — from 'hippy-dippy' to 'tax us all to death' to 'marry his own dog' — all delivered as proud endorsements
jokes.explanation: The escalation from slightly dismissive terms to 'make it legal for a man to marry his own dog' is classic 30 Rock political satire. Jack is being genuinely romantic while using the most extreme right-wing characterization of liberal positions. The cognitive dissonance is the joke.

jokes.text: First executive, unprompted, stands up: 'I gave to NPR last year.'
jokes.setup: Jack has just declared his love for a liberal congresswoman in front of his conservative peers
jokes.punchline: One executive immediately confesses his own liberal apostasy — NPR donation — as if Jack's announcement has opened a confessional
jokes.explanation: The confessional escalation sequence is the episode's comedic climax and is perfectly constructed. 'I gave to NPR last year' is the ideal first domino — small enough to be pathetic, large enough to be a genuine confession for this room. The structure of the sequence is exceptional.

jokes.text: Second executive: 'My children go to public school.'
jokes.setup: The confessional sequence is building
jokes.punchline: Public school attendance as a deep shame for a corporate executive — the second beat escalates the absurdity of what counts as a guilty secret in this room
jokes.explanation: The perfect escalation beat. NPR was embarrassing but small; public school is a bigger class-betrayal for these executives. The sequence is building to something bigger.

jokes.text: Second executive confession: 'My children go to public school.'
jokes.setup: The confessional cascade is building
jokes.punchline: Public school as a shameful secret among NBC executives — the horror of non-elite education for their children
jokes.explanation: The escalation from NPR to public school is perfect — it's not more liberal, it's just more economically revealing. These executives treat middle-class choices as moral failures. Economy is exceptional — four words, maximum social satire.

jokes.text: Third executive: 'I'm gay.' Fourth executive: 'I'm black.'
jokes.setup: The confessional sequence continues escalating
jokes.punchline: From NPR to public school to 'I'm gay' to 'I'm black' — the 'confessions' have stopped being choices and become fundamental identities, which these executives have apparently been hiding
jokes.explanation: The genius of this beat: the sequence has established 'liberal sins' as the confession format, then pivots to fundamental human identities being treated as equivalent shameful secrets in this corporate environment. 'I'm gay' and 'I'm black' as corporate confessions is both funny and devastating social satire. The escalation structure is flawless — each beat tops the last.

jokes.text: And I just want you to know that, in 1984, I voted for Ronald Reagan.
jokes.setup: Jack has just made a brave, loving public declaration; the sequence is at emotional peak
jokes.punchline: C.C.'s emotional reciprocation takes the form of a political confession: she voted for Reagan in 1984 — a massive liberal apostasy delivered with the same gravity as the identity confessions
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's two best jokes. The structure is perfect: Jack has made a genuinely vulnerable declaration, C.C. reciprocates with her own confession of equal intimacy — and it's a 1984 Reagan vote. It works on every level: (1) it recontextualizes C.C.'s political identity, (2) it's the exact equivalent of Jack's confession in the other direction, (3) the room's reaction (which must be seismic given the escalating confessions) is implied. The specificity of '1984' is perfect — not just 'I voted for Reagan' but pinning it to the year of his landslide. Exceptional structure and character integration.

jokes.text: Final executive stands up last: 'I murdered my wife.'
jokes.setup: The confessional sequence has gone from NPR → public school → gay → Black
jokes.punchline: The final confession is actual murder — which lands as the funniest beat because the sequence has normalized increasing severity, and this is both a complete non sequitur AND the logical endpoint of the escalation
jokes.explanation: The episode's best single punchline and one of 30 Rock's all-time great joke endings. The entire confessional sequence has been building a comedy logic: 'shameful secrets in a conservative corporate environment.' NPR-public school-gay-Black have escalated the stakes, and then 'I murdered my wife' is the terminal point. It's the perfect final beat because (a) it's structurally the only thing that tops 'I'm Black' in this particular sequence, (b) it's three words, (c) no one reacts, (d) it implies this man has been waiting for an opportunity to confess and this seemed like the moment. Maximum economy, maximum impact. Justifies top scores.

tmdb_overview: C.C. and Jack face a block in their relationship when C.C. decides to go public about the affair but Jack refuses. Meanwhile, Liz struggles to keep both Tracy and Jenna happy when the two find it hard to share the spotlight, while Frank makes fun of Toofer's Harvard education with bizarre results.
insight: Absurdist chaos drives 71 jokes in 23 minutes — barely missed elite tier.
